items.title: Water availability mediates the effectiveness of precision and bet‐hedging seeding strategies in wetland restoration
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Hydrologic extremes such as drought are projected to intensify with climate change, challenging wetland revegetation. Seed‐based restoration is widely used because it is cost‐effective and scalable, but establishment often fails under unsuitable moisture conditions. Two frameworks may improve outcomes under uncertainty: precision restoration, which matches treatments to site conditions, and bet‐hedging, which diversifies strategies to spread risk. These approaches remain largely untested in wetlands.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To compare the effects of precision and bet‐hedging seeding strategies on plant community recovery in wetland restoration.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We evaluated one precision treatment (5‐species mix) and three bet‐hedging treatments: a diverse species mix, delayed germination, and multi‐year sowing at two hydrologically distinct sites in Great Salt Lake wetlands, Utah, United States. We measured native and invasive plant cover, community composition, and labor and seed costs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Hydrology dominated restoration outcomes. At Farmington Bay, rapid drying suppressed establishment across all treatments, indicating that neither strategy can overcome severe moisture limitation. At Howard Slough, where soils remained saturated, the precision treatment produced the highest seeded cover in year one. By year 2, seeded cover converged across treatments, but multi‐year sowing reduced invasive cover relative to the unseeded control. Precision and diverse mix treatments required the least labor, whereas multi‐year sowing required approximately 3× more effort but provided the strongest ecological benefits over time.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Water availability strongly constrains seed‐based wetland revegetation. Precision approaches promote rapid establishment under favorable conditions, whereas repeated sowing can improve longer‐term outcomes by reducing invasive cover, albeit with greater labor demands.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

items.title: Native grass cover as a field indicator of mycorrhizal inoculum potential in southwestern drylands
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Drylands experience disturbances that can lead to shifts in plant and microbial communities. Arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) fungi help mediate establishment, survival, and resource flow within above‐ and belowground communities and have the potential to be used as a restoration tool to facilitate revegetation under disturbance regimes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To better understand how AM fungal abundance changes with disturbance and examine its restoration potential, we sampled soils across a gradient of sites in the southwestern United States. We hypothesized that (1) AM fungal abundance would be greater in “Reference” compared to “Disturbed” areas, and (2) plant functional group cover at the sampling source would help predict AM fungal abundance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      At six sites, we sampled soil and measured plant functional group cover from paired areas that had documented disturbance with low native plant cover (“Disturbed”) and no or low disturbance with high native plant cover (“Reference”). We compared the mycorrhizal inoculum potential (MIP), a measure of the density of viable propagules of AM fungi, in these soils using two greenhouse bioassays: one with 120
                      <jats:italic>Bouteloua gracilis</jats:italic>
                      plants and the other with 120
                      <jats:italic>Zea mays</jats:italic>
                      plants.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      MIP was greater in Reference than Disturbed areas at five of the six sites in the
                      <jats:italic>B. gracilis</jats:italic>
                      bioassay. Native grass cover was strongly positively correlated with MIP.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These results suggest that both disturbance and plant functional group can help predict MIP, and that the presence of native grass seems to consistently correlate with MIP across a range of dryland contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

items.title: Cost‐effective assessment of forest restoration projects: merging advanced techniques with comprehensive analysis
items.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Forest restoration projects affect the entire ecosystem; therefore, they require comprehensive environmental monitoring to ensure their success and counteract unexpected challenges. In this context, complementary monitoring indicators should be selected based on available budget and time, along with advanced analytical techniques to enable a cost‐effective, more comprehensive evaluation of ecosystem outcomes. Here, we describe how measuring tree community composition, aboveground biomass of trees, soil nutrients, and soil microbes using high‐throughput sequencing can provide a broader understanding of the restoration trajectory, especially when environmental variables are considered together using machine learning algorithms. As a successful example of this approach, we report the results of a case study conducted in naturally regenerating
                    <jats:italic>Acacia mangium</jats:italic>
                    plantations. Ultimately, this research serves as a robust baseline and validation of the efficiency of advanced techniques for studying complementary indicators of forest restoration across forest biomes and geographic regions.
                  </jats:p>

items.title: Nursery fertilization shapes physiological drought responses but does not enhance field survival in Cryptocarya alba from Mediterranean central Chile
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>High seedling mortality during the establishment phase remains a major constraint for forest restoration in Mediterranean‐type ecosystems, where increasing drought frequency and intensity limit post‐planting performance. Seedling survival under these conditions depends not only on site characteristics and species selection but also on functional traits acquired during nursery cultivation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We evaluated whether reducing nursery fertilization induces functional traits and physiological responses associated with drought tolerance, and whether these responses improve field survival of
                      <jats:italic>Cryptocarya alba</jats:italic>
                      , a native Mediterranean tree species widely used in restoration programs in central Chile.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Seedlings were grown under contrasting fertilization regimes, exposed to a controlled drought experiment, and subsequently outplanted across contrasting slope aspects representing different levels of water limitation. Morphological traits, physiological responses, and post‐planting survival were assessed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Reduced fertilization altered seedling morphology and biomass allocation and, particularly under low nitrogen (low N) availability, allowed seedlings to maintain photosynthetic activity under drought. However, these responses did not translate into improved field survival. Control seedlings showed higher final survival than seedlings grown under low N and low nitrogen–phosphorus fertilization, whereas the low phosphorus treatment did not differ significantly from the control. Survival also differed between slope aspects and among restoration sites, but the fertilization × slope interaction was not significant.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Physiological responses to drought induced during nursery cultivation were insufficient to improve field establishment when accompanied by substantial reductions in seedling growth. For
                      <jats:italic>C. alba</jats:italic>
                      , reduced nursery fertilization therefore provided no advantage for post‐planting survival under the conditions evaluated.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

items.title: Responses of peatland waders to large‐scale, non‐native forestry removal: measuring changes in edge effects after 20 years
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Restoration of afforested peatlands aims to recover biodiversity, but evidence for long‐term bird responses remains limited. In Scotland's Flow Country, conifer plantations established during the 1970s and 1980s displaced breeding waders and created edge effects on adjacent bog. Forest‐to‐bog restoration began in the 1990s and expanded during the 2000s.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To assess whether relationships between breeding wader occupancy and historical forest edges differ between standing plantations and areas where forest has been removed for restoration.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We surveyed 171 km
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      of open peatland during 2022–2024, approximately two decades after an earlier survey. We recorded 1951 species‐by‐square occurrences of Dunlin (
                      <jats:italic>Calidris alpina</jats:italic>
                      ), Golden plover (
                      <jats:italic>Pluvialis apricaria</jats:italic>
                      ), and Greenshank (
                      <jats:italic>Tringa nebularia</jats:italic>
                      ). Presence–absence models assessed associations with forest proximity, environmental characteristics, and historical forest edge status.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Golden plover showed a weaker occupancy relationship with distance from restoration edges than standing‐forest edges. Dunlin showed a similar pattern, although evidence for differing distance relationships was weaker. Forest proximity remained associated with occupancy for both species. Greenshank showed limited evidence of a strong overall forest edge effect.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Contemporary occupancy patterns are consistent with reduced historical forest edge effects following plantation removal, particularly for Golden plover. However, these observational comparisons cannot establish causal effects or directly quantify temporal occupancy change.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
